name: Carpotarsal Osteochondromatosis
aliases: Osteochondromatosis of Carpal and Tarsal Bones

criteria.description: Presence of multiple osteochondromas predominantly affecting carpal and tarsal bones
Early onset skeletal deformities including short stature and joint contractures
Radiographic evidence of irregular ossification and osteochondral lesions in carpal and tarsal bones
Positive family history consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance
Absence of metaphyseal involvement typical of hereditary multiple exostoses

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of multiple osteochondromas in carpal and tarsal bones with radiographic confirmation and early-onset skeletal deformities
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Genetic testing may assist but is not definitive; diagnosis primarily clinical and radiological

laboratory: No specific laboratory abnormalities; routine blood tests typically normal
imaging: X-rays showing multiple osteochondromas predominantly in carpal and tarsal bones
Irregular ossification and joint space narrowing on radiographs
MRI may show cartilage cap thickness and soft tissue involvement
genetic: Mutations in EXT1 or EXT2 genes may be identified but not consistently
Genetic testing useful to differentiate from hereditary multiple exostoses
other: Clinical examination revealing joint contractures and deformities
Family history suggestive of autosomal dominant inheritance pattern

distinguishingFeatures: Osteochondromas primarily affecting metaphyses of long bones
Wider distribution of lesions beyond carpal and tarsal bones
Generalized skeletal dysplasia with different radiographic features
Lack of typical carpal and tarsal osteochondromas

redFlags: Rapid increase in size of osteochondromas suggesting malignant transformation
Severe joint contractures causing functional impairment
Neurological deficits due to nerve compression
references: Schmale GA, Conrad EU, Raskind WH. The natural history of hereditary multiple exostoses. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1994
